An adverbial clause is a group of words which have the same function as an adverb. Like all clauses, an adverbial clause has a subject and a verb.

Adverbial clauses of time are used to express when something happens or how often something happens.
You can use a subordinating conjunction like after, as, as long as, as soon as or until to introduce the adverbial clause.

Example:
I'm going to register to my local gym as soon as I get paid.
I'll train until I start seeing results.

Defining Relative Clauses as Subject and Object

You use relative clauses to join two separate clauses into one sentence. You can also use relative clauses to give more information about something.
A defining relative clause gives information about a noun. You need this information to know which noun we are talking about.
A defining relative clause can either be used as subject or object.

When the relative pronoun is the subject, the relative clause can come after the subject or the object of the sentence. You can't drop the relative pronoun.
Example:
I'm looking for a gym that is near my apartment.
The people who train at this gym are all athletes.

When the relative pronoun is the object, we can drop the relative pronoun if we want to. The clause can come after the subject or the object of the sentence.
Example:
The gym (that) I go to has recently shut down.
While I was at the gym, I met an athlete (who) I went to school with.

images.text: Until fairly recently, athletes did not put much of an emphasis on physical fitness. Babe Ruth, the baseball legend who set the single-season home run record, was notoriously overweight. Batting champion Wade Boggs used to eat fried chicken before each game. And golfer John Daly would smoke cigarettes in the middle of a competition!

This all changed when athletes like Tiger Woods and Jose Canseco developed training regimens which gave them a competitive edge over their contemporaries. When Canseco, a baseball player for the Oakland Athletics, was training for the season, he would run several kilometres to the gym, do a full workout, and then run home. His physical fitness allowed him to possess the rare combination of power and speed that set him apart from the rest of the league. Tiger Woods also credited much of his early success to his dedication to physical conditioning. The increased body mass and strength that resulted from his training allowed him to hit the golf ball farther than any other professional golfer.
As soon as Jose Canseco and Tiger Woods started finding success, people who had never lifted a weight before began hitting the gym. Once this became the norm, those who had put off training got left in the dust. The era of the self-made athlete had begun.

In modern basketball, plyometric training has made it impossible for large, plodding giants to keep up with the sleek, well-conditioned youngsters who are currently dominating the league.
And the demanding training schedule that most hockey players follow has made the game bigger, faster and more exciting. The harsh truth is that if you're a 21st century athlete and you're out of shape, you're out of a job!
